After announcing changes to App Tracking Transparency in Europe, Apple is now introducing a simplified App Store commission structure for developers in the region. Here are the details.

Apple Revises Business Terms for EU App Developers

Apple previously announced eight changes to App Tracking Transparency in Europe, following an investigation by Germany's antitrust regulator.

The company is now announcing a new commission structure for the region taking effect October 1, including reducing the external link commission to 15% and replacing the controversial "Core Technology Fee" with a 5% "Core Technology Commission."

This comes just over a year after Apple announced sweeping revisions to the EU App Store, when Apple introduced a complex set of rules—details here.

Here is Apple's statement:

Apple is also announcing new terms for App Store commission rates, alternative app payment options, and distributing apps through alternative app marketplaces or the web.

The new terms are as follows:

For App Store apps using Apple's in-app purchase system, the commission will be 26%. For the vast majority of developers—including those in the App Store Small Business Partner Program, Mini Program Partner Program, or Video Partner Program, as well as subscriptions that auto-renew after the first year—the commission will be 15%. For App Store apps using alternative payment processing, the commission will be 20%. Developers in the aforementioned programs will be eligible for a reduced rate of 10%. For App Store apps that link out to an external website to complete a purchase, the commission will be 15%. Developers in the aforementioned programs will be eligible for a reduced rate of 10%. For apps distributed through alternative app marketplaces or the web, Apple will charge a 5% Core Technology Commission.

Under the new terms, developers may also offer both Apple in-app purchase and alternative payment options, either in-app or via an external website link, provided they comply with Apple's "presentation requirements" and maintain their chosen payment option for no less than 12 months.

The announcement also includes new protections for children's safety and rules regarding alternative payment options in the EU:

Apps in the "Kids" category on the App Store will not be allowed to contain links that direct users to an external website to complete a transaction, in order to reduce the risk of fraud or scams targeting children. For users under 18, all App Store apps that use alternative payment processing or link out to an external website for transactions must have a parental gate in place, requiring a parent or guardian's involvement before a young user can make a purchase. For users under 13, App Store apps cannot link out to an external website to complete a transaction, to prevent fraud risks targeting young children.

Apple added that in EU member states where parental consent is required for digital activities for children over 13 as well, "these protections will be adjusted accordingly."

Finally, the changes announced today by Apple also expand eligibility for operating alternative app marketplaces or distributing apps via the web.

The expanded eligibility criteria include:

Meeting a moderate level of financial standing as rated by Dun & Bradstreet. Being a publicly traded company or owned by one. Having received venture capital funding from a reputable investment firm. Completing a financial audit conducted by a licensed accounting firm. Being a government agency, educational institution, or non-profit organization.

Apple noted that the web distribution method currently offered only in the EU lacks the ongoing oversight provided by app marketplace operators, potentially allowing bad actors to "operate for long periods before being discovered, harming users."

As a result, Apple says it will continue to require all apps distributed through alternative channels to go through its Notarization review process.

For more on today's announcement, tap here.

Update: A European Commission spokesperson told Bloomberg that the Commission welcomed Apple's changes, calling the measures the result of "close dialogue." The spokesperson added that the Commission will monitor Apple's implementation of the new terms.

What do you think about Apple's new rules for the EU? Let us know in the comments.
